video.title: He Re-Invented this Oversaturated Business (And Makes $3M/Year)

summary: Stanley Henry describes how he built The Attention Seeker from a LinkedIn personal-brand service into an organic social agency for large brands and solo operators. He explains how the agency tests repeatable content formats, why it gives new series time to find an audience, and how it uses AI to reduce coordination work while keeping creative production human-led. He also describes a newer education business selling webinars and digital products to the audience he built. The main takeaway is to earn attention with a simple, entertaining story, test consistently, and add sales messaging only after the content has proved itself.

speakers.name: David Heacock
speakers.description: Host of the Boring Money podcast, identified by the channel name.

ideas.name: The Attention Seeker organic social media agency
ideas.one_liner: Creates and runs organic social campaigns for brands, using content designed to earn attention without relying on paid distribution.
ideas.business_model: Client services; agency engagements and retainers. Specific prices are not stated.
ideas.customer: Brands, especially large or boring businesses such as banks, telecoms, energy companies, insurance companies, and product businesses. Also works with underdogs and some personal brands.
ideas.problem: Brands struggle to get attention and positive feelings for products people may find boring, dislike, or only think about when they need them.
ideas.offer: Develop a social content strategy and repeatable series, then produce and manage organic content across platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, and podcasts. The agency may later add paid distribution or calls to action.

pricing.model: Agency client engagement or retainer; exact pricing not stated.
pricing.notes: The host says the initial Filterby engagement was a three-month engagement, but its price is not stated.

acquisition_channels.details: The agency demonstrates its own work through content on its channels; prospects see the proof and approach the agency.

quote.text: And kind of the way brands find us is like the proof's in the pudding. They've they've seen us. They've seen our content.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

acquisition_channels.details: Clients and people in Stanley's network introduced opportunities; some clients had been watching the agency's content before contacting it.
After moving back to New Zealand, Stanley built a network through frequent coffee meetings and networking events; some early clients came from people he had met in person.

ideas.delivery: The team develops content concepts and campaigns, interviews clients to find real stories, and makes content for their channels. Creators and editors handle much of the production; journalists interview some clients. AI handles much of the project coordination, briefing, and proposal or pitch preparation. Video editing remains mostly human, with AI used for tasks such as sound cleanup and podcast camera switching.
unit_economics_claims: Stanley says the agency had about 15 staff after starting with LinkedIn personal branding and later grew to 40 people before reducing to about 15.
Stanley says the agency now has more revenue and is more profitable than it was 18 months earlier, without giving amounts.
Stanley says the agency's TikTok account reached 300,000 followers within about three months and about 700,000 followers roughly a year and a half later.
Stanley says the agency reached 300,000 Instagram followers about two months after starting to focus on Instagram.
Stanley says Pizza Hut New Zealand grew from about 3,000 followers to about 100,000 across its platforms over three years.
Stanley says the agency's current proposition can be to get a client five million views a month from posting, without ad spend; this is a sales claim, not a guaranteed result.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. The agency already had suitable computers, graphics cards, and a large local server for its content work.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. The agency started receiving requests for LinkedIn help after Stanley spent about six months building a network and posting content; the exact time to first revenue is not stated.

acquisition.how: Agents can help create, schedule, and analyze agency content, but attracting and closing high-value brand clients still depends on strong creative proof, relationships, and human sales.

onboarding.how: Call recordings can feed proposals and briefs, but agreeing a client's brand, audience, and creative direction needs human judgment.

delivery.how: The offer depends on human storytelling, interviews, filming, and editing. AI assists with coordination and production tasks, but the guest says editing remains mostly human.

billing.how: Recurring invoices and payment follow-up could be automated, but the transcript does not describe the billing system.

support.how: AI can prepare updates and briefs, while client feedback, approvals, and creative discussions need human involvement.

uk_applicability.notes: The platforms and agency model work in the UK. Content production and client acquisition still require human creative work; there is no transcript-specific US-only dependency.

risks: Organic reach may take months to develop, and clients may give up after only a short trial.
The agency is people-intensive because the guest says strong content still needs human creators and editors.
Social platforms and their algorithms change, so a format or tactic can become saturated.
The guest describes agencies as difficult to scale and says cash flow can be challenging.
Starting too many channels or series at once can split attention and starve promising work of resources.
Overediting and relying on viral tricks can make content feel forced; the guest says simple stories perform better.

ideas.name: LinkedIn personal-brand management service
ideas.one_liner: Writes LinkedIn content for founders, brokers, and business leaders to help them grow their reach and referral networks online.
ideas.business_model: Client services for personal-brand content; exact fee structure not stated.
ideas.customer: Solo entrepreneurs, brokers and other small-business owners, and leaders at midsize B2B businesses or businesses involving substantial purchases such as mortgages.
ideas.problem: Customers rely heavily on referrals and their existing networks and want to extend that reach digitally.
ideas.offer: Manage a person's LinkedIn brand by writing text posts and producing pictures with text. The service later expanded into video and other platforms.

pricing.model: Client services; exact pricing not stated.
pricing.notes: Stanley says the LinkedIn service funded the agency's first three years but gives no client prices.

acquisition_channels.details: Stanley first built his own LinkedIn personal brand and used the results to demonstrate the service.
Stanley met people in person while rebuilding his New Zealand network; people he met later asked for help with LinkedIn.
The service helped customers scale their referral networks digitally; early demand came from people in Stanley's network.

ideas.delivery: The agency wrote text posts and supplied pictures with text for clients' LinkedIn profiles. The transcript does not describe a detailed production workflow or staffing for this service.
unit_economics_claims: Stanley says LinkedIn personal branding was the agency's sole focus for its first three years and that the company had about 15 staff at that point.
Stanley says the service was quite profitable and funded the agency for its first three years; no amounts are stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. After six months of networking and posting content, people asked Stanley for LinkedIn help during lockdown.

acquisition.how: Publishing useful examples and personal-brand content can attract inbound clients, but the guest's early customer development also relied on in-person networking and relationships.

onboarding.how: An intake form and AI-assisted interview summaries could collect background, but positioning a leader's voice and goals requires human judgment.

delivery.how: Drafting and scheduling can be assisted by agents, but the guest's current approach emphasizes real interviews and authentic stories that need human input.

billing.how: Recurring billing can be automated, though no billing process is described.

support.how: AI could handle routine updates, but revisions and voice or reputation concerns require human review.

uk_applicability.notes: LinkedIn personal-brand services can be sold and delivered in the UK. B2B positioning and writing may need to reflect local industries and audience expectations.

risks: The service depends on clients sharing authentic stories and approving content in their own voice.
LinkedIn content can become repetitive or AI-like if it relies on generic rewriting instead of real interviews.
The transcript gives no pricing, margins, or client counts for this service.

quotes.text: we were purely personal branding on LinkedIn for first three years of the business and we got to about 15 staff at that point.

ideas.name: Social media and AI education products
ideas.one_liner: Sells education through weekly webinars and digital products to an existing audience interested in AI, social media content, and Meta ads.
ideas.business_model: Digital products and education sold to an existing audience, with webinar delivery and upsells.
ideas.customer: The agency's followers and people interested in AI, social media content, and Meta ads; the business had initially sold mainly to New Zealand and Australian customers.
ideas.problem: Customers want practical education on AI and social media topics the agency uses in its own work.
ideas.offer: Stanley creates content about what the business does, uses it to attract interest, and sells education through a two-hour webinar each week, digital products, and upsells delivered with contract staff.

pricing.model: Paid digital products and education, with upsells; specific product price stated for one offer.
pricing.notes: The guest does not state the product's currency. The webinar itself is described as the main delivery point; its standalone price is not stated.

acquisition_channels.details: Stanley posts about AI, content, and Meta ads on Instagram; a post that performs well is used as the basis for paid promotion.
The guest says they put money behind content that receives many comments and scale the ads when sales are working.
The business launched education to an audience that Stanley says already followed the brand and its personal account.

ideas.delivery: Stanley presents a two-hour webinar every week as the main delivery point. Contract staff deliver upsells. The guest says the same webinar format can accommodate a much larger audience without changing the work.
unit_economics_claims: Stanley says the education business brings in about a quarter of a million per month from New Zealand and Australia; the currency is not stated.
Stanley says a product priced at $190 had a customer acquisition cost of about $40; the currency is not explicitly stated.
Stanley says the weekly webinar takes two hours of his time and upsells are delivered by contract staff.
Stanley says the webinar could serve 50 people or 5,000 with the same work.
The opening montage includes a first-month figure of 150 after an expected 20 or 30 grand; the clipped remark does not clearly identify the business or currency.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. The guest says education was easy to launch because the business already had an audience.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: The guest says the education business began about three months before the interview and took off quickly; exact time to first revenue is not stated.

acquisition.how: Agents can repurpose posts, run paid campaigns, and track conversions, while a human still needs to choose good content and oversee advertising.

onboarding.how: Purchases and access to recorded or live webinar materials can be handled by software; questions about a buyer's goals may need human help.

delivery.how: A live weekly webinar currently depends on Stanley, and upsells use contract staff. Recorded material could reduce delivery work, but that is not the described core offer.

billing.how: Digital checkout, payment, and access can be automated, though the guest does not describe the payment stack.

support.how: Agents could answer routine product and access questions; coaching or nuanced questions may need a person.

uk_applicability.notes: Webinars and digital products can be sold from the UK. Content and pricing may need adjustment for UK audiences, but the transcript describes no US-only platform or legal dependency.

risks: The business depends on the founder's audience and personal brand for demand.
The webinar still uses two hours of the founder's time each week.
Customer acquisition cost and product price are stated without currency, period, sample size, or margin detail.

tactics.name: Build proof on your own channels before selling the service
steps: Choose a platform and post consistently about the work and your journey.
Use your own account to test formats and show prospective clients what you can do.
Let prospects see the work and do their own due diligence before approaching you.

quote.text: our whole like I guess philosophy is first we do it for ourselves and then we prove it and then we do it for clients.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

tactics.name: Build an initial professional network through frequent in-person meetings
steps: After returning to a market where you lack a network, post about the journey and meet as many relevant people as possible.
Stanley held five to six coffee meetings a day and attended networking events for six months.
Keep in touch and respond when people ask for help with the skill you have been demonstrating.

quote.text: So for 6 months straight, I just like had five to six coffee meetings with people every day.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

tactics.name: Test a new platform by hiring platform-native talent
steps: When TikTok looked promising, Stanley hired a creator with a large TikTok following.
Ask the creator to make content for the company account while learning what works on the platform.
Use the results and platform knowledge to decide whether to expand.

quote.text: Let's learn how this works. Try make us content as our brand and then we'll try to learn what's working on the platform
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

tactics.name: Give a new internal content creator a measurable production target
steps: Hire an internal creator whose full-time job is making content.
Set a target of five videos a day and give the person six months to learn.
Ask for a weekly report covering what they did, learned, and will start, stop, and continue.
Review progress and add specialist guidance only after the creator has tested enough content.

quote.text: every week you need to tell me what you did, what you learned, what you going to start, stop, continue.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

tactics.name: Make a local business recognisable to its target area
steps: Make the location clear in the content, including naming the town or area served.
Publish consistently so platforms can test the content with a local audience.
Judge results by local reach and the credibility or calls it creates, not just viral view counts.

quote.text: if you mention I'm the number one, you know, plumbing business in West Palm Beach, then like it's going to show to people in West Palm Beach.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

tactics.name: Let an organic series establish audience interest before adding sales calls to action
steps: Start with one repeatable series designed to entertain or create a feeling associated with the brand.
Keep the early format consistent and allow it time to find an audience.
After the characters and format have established interest, add service or product content and calls to action.
Put paid distribution behind content that already shows audience interest.

quote.text: the first three month engagement is just get the show to be loved and once we've done that and we prove it then we can look at the next tier of stuff
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

tactics.name: Keep early creative tests simple
steps: Start with the core story and use the simplest edit that communicates it.
Avoid adding hooks, effects, and editing tricks before the basic story has been tested.
Use early results to decide which extra elements are worth adding.

quote.text: The videos that we're putting live on your channel uh this afternoon are as the simplest possible edit we can do.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

tactics.name: Use content that performs organically as the basis for paid campaigns
steps: Post content about the work and products.
Identify a post that receives strong comments or other engagement.
Use that post in a paid campaign and increase spend when sales are working.

quote.text: one that goes well, we do the mini chat automation and one that gets lots of comments, we just put money behind it
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

tactics.name: Launch education to an audience you have already built
steps: Use an existing audience to test whether people will buy a practical product based on your company's work.
Begin with a webinar and digital products that are quick to launch.
Use early customer acquisition results to decide whether to scale the offer and target new markets.

quote.text: We just thought it's easy to spin up. We can test if our audience actually buys from us.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

tactics.name: Use AI to turn conversations into proposals and internal briefs
steps: Record client or prospect calls.
Feed the transcript into the agency's AI context system.
Have the system prepare a proposal or creative pitch so the team can spend more time discussing ideas.
Use AI to prompt staff with the briefs and tasks needed for its work.

quote.text: that phone call can be recorded and then the AI can just spit out the proposal straight afterwards
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

tactics.name: Add a new channel or content series one at a time
steps: Choose one new platform, channel, or series.
Put the team's attention and resources into getting that one working.
Expand to another audience or series after the first has a stable format.

quote.text: every time we're going to go into a new platform and a new channel, let's just only do that. put all our effort into that
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

warnings.warning: Organic content usually takes time to work. Stanley says some small businesses give up after only two weeks, while he recommends giving it three to six months.

quote.text: What usually happens with a lot of small businesses, they'll do it for two weeks and they're like, "Oh, this didn't work, did it?"
quote.speaker: David Heacock

warnings.warning: Paid spend cannot reliably rescue content that people do not want to watch; weak content can become expensive to distribute.

quote.text: you can't pay um Facebook to distribute crap anymore because they don't want people to to jump off of it
quote.speaker: David Heacock

warnings.warning: Trying too many platforms or series at once can split attention and leave some work without the resources it needs.

quote.text: And because your mind gets split and you'll also like something will work and then you'll favor that and not the other one
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

warnings.warning: The agency still relies on people for strong creative production; Stanley says AI editing is not yet good enough for the quality his business needs.

quote.text: We won't actually like have it fully edit on its own. Um we actually just think our editors are just faster at the moment still and better.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

warnings.warning: Social content built from cheap tricks, excessive editing, or overly complicated execution can lose the story and feel inauthentic.

quote.text: actually like the best thing to do is to strip out like strip out as much as you can.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

warnings.warning: Agency work can generate cash flow but is difficult to scale and can have cash-flow challenges.

quote.text: And cash flow as well. cash flow as well.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

quote.text: We thought we do 20, 30 grand in first month, and first month was 150.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

lessons.lesson: Demonstrate your service on your own channels so prospects can see evidence of your work before they buy.

quote.text: first we do it for ourselves and then we prove it and then we do it for clients.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

lessons.lesson: For social content, a real and relatable story is more durable than a short-lived hook or editing trick.

quote.text: if you can tell a good story, you know, a proper setup conflict resolution in in every story you tell, you'll find an audience.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

lessons.lesson: Test with enough volume to learn, but keep the process simple so you can see what is working.

quote.text: The videos that we're putting live on your channel uh this afternoon are as the simplest possible edit we can do.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

lessons.lesson: Treat organic social as a long-term channel and give a new format time to find its audience.

quote.text: So, if you're out there and you're going to try it, just give it give it time. Give it three to six months.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

lessons.lesson: Build an entertaining series first; introduce product messages and calls to action after people care about the format.

quote.text: get the show to be loved and once we've done that and we prove it then we can look at the next tier of stuff
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

lessons.lesson: AI can take over coordination and routine document work, but the agency keeps humans in the creative work that needs high quality.

quote.text: the two things we do in our business is conversations and content. um everything else
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

lessons.lesson: Create separate channels or series for different audience segments instead of forcing every audience into one format.

quote.text: you don't have to have one series on one channel. you know, Nike has 100.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

lessons.lesson: Focus resources on one new platform or series at a time, then expand after it works.

quote.text: every time we're going to go into a new platform and a new channel, let's just only do that. put all our effort into that
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

lessons.lesson: An agency can build skills, relationships, and cash flow that later support a more scalable product business.

quote.text: I knew the agency wasn't scalable. I can get it to be very good cash flow, very profitable um and then use that extra cash flow
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

lessons.lesson: A business audience can be a low-friction place to test whether customers will pay for educational products.

quote.text: We just thought it's easy to spin up. We can test if our audience actually buys from us.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

lessons.lesson: When using AI in a company, capture useful business context from real conversations and documents, then make it available to the team.

quote.text: we've been recording like uh meetings for the last three years with Otter and all our emails and all our like documents
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

lessons.lesson: Make content easy to understand in the first moments because people scroll quickly and have little patience for complicated setups.

quote.text: the simpler it is, the easier it will come across. The more human it is, the more simple it comes across
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

evidence_quality.rationale: The guest is an operator describing his own agency, staffing, content process, tools, and education business. He gives several concrete audience, staffing, timing, and acquisition figures, but many financial claims lack currency, definitions, supporting records, or detail about profitability. One opening revenue figure is clipped and ambiguous.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host says Filterby hired Stanley's agency for a project, so part of the interview also serves as a client case study. The guest discusses his own education products and agency but does not make a direct course pitch in this transcript.
